result: The old lighthouse keeper swore the sea kept secrets better than any vault. Each night he climbed the spiral stairs, lantern in hand, listening to the waves argue with the rocks below. Salt crusted his beard and the iron railing, yet he never tired of the ritual. Far out, a freighter’s lights blinked like distant thoughts, and he wondered what cargo it carried—grain, machines, or simply the weight of someone else’s hope. He had once been a sailor himself, chasing horizons until the horizons chased him back. Now the beam he tended swept the water in slow, faithful arcs, warning others away from the very edges he had loved. On clear evenings the stars arrived early, and he named them after people he had lost, as if light could keep a promise the body could not. When storms came he stayed awake, not from duty alone but from a stubborn affection for the noise. Rain hammered the glass; wind tried the door. In those hours the keeper felt most alive, small and necessary at once. Morning always returned, pale and ordinary, gulls rewriting the sky. He descended, boiled coffee, and wrote nothing in the log except “all well.” The sea, he knew, would keep the rest.
